prompt: Which shape of problem does this lesson say an agent is for?

choices.text: When the path cannot be written down in advance
choices.why: Right. When the next step depends on what the last one found, a fixed path cannot be written.

choices.text: Any task in which a language model takes part somewhere
choices.why: Workflows use models too. Section 04 names five patterns that do and are not agents.

choices.text: Tasks with a lot of traffic, where speed matters most
choices.why: Volume argues for a workflow: the agent's cost grows with every message.

choices.text: Questions with one known answer
choices.why: A known answer is the clearest case for a fixed path.

prompt: Which test from the lesson tells you, quickly, whether a task has an agent's shape?

choices.text: Whether customers will read it
choices.why: Who reads the output is a deployment choice. It says nothing about the path.

choices.text: Whether a new hire could follow a written procedure without judgement
choices.why: Right. If they could, a workflow can follow it too.

choices.text: Whether the task currently takes a person more than an hour each time
choices.why: Long tasks with a fixed path are still workflows, and often the best ones to automate.

choices.text: Whether a model is good at it
choices.why: Being good at something does not mean the path has to be chosen at run time.

prompt: Why are coding assistants that edit and run code in a loop such a natural fit for an agent?

choices.text: Because source code is short enough to fit in any model's context window
choices.why: Many code bases are far too large for that, and the agent reads files one at a time for exactly that reason.

choices.text: Because programmers trust models more than other people do
choices.why: Trust is not what makes the shape fit. The shape is about the path.

choices.text: The next file to read depends on the last one, and tests check the result
choices.why: Right. The path is unknown in advance and the outcome is checkable, which is the combination section 03 asks for.

choices.text: Code changes are always reversible
choices.why: Some are, with version control. But a deploy, a migration or a deleted branch is not.

prompt: A task's result can only be judged by somebody who reads all the sources the agent read. What does that do to the case for an agent?

choices.text: Nothing: checking is a separate job from doing
choices.why: If the checker repeats the work, the work was not saved. Checkability is one of the four questions for that reason.

choices.text: It strengthens it, because a person is reviewing anyway
choices.why: A person reviewing everything turns the agent into an assistant with extra steps.

choices.text: It weakens it: the saving shrinks to almost nothing
choices.why: Right. The third question asks whether checking a result is cheaper than producing it.

choices.text: It means the task needs a bigger model
choices.why: The size of the model does not change who has to read the sources.

prompt: A support queue gets 20,000 messages a day; nine in ten fit a handful of known procedures. Which design does the lesson point to?

choices.text: An agent for every message, so that all of them get the same quality of answer
choices.why: That pays the agent's cost on the nine in ten a fixed path already answers.

choices.text: A router for the known procedures, and an agent or a person for the rest
choices.why: Right. The two are not exclusive; the router's leftovers are where the agent earns its cost.

choices.text: A router only, discarding the messages it cannot classify
choices.why: Discarding a tenth of the queue loses the cases that most need help.

choices.text: No model at all
choices.why: Reading a message to pick a procedure is a fair job for one model call.

prompt: Match each pattern to what it does.

pairs.right: One call's output is the next call's input
One call picks a fixed branch
Several calls on one input, combined by code
One call writes, another judges, until accepted

right_distractors: The model chooses which tools exist

prompt: Of the five patterns, which sits closest to an agent, and why?

choices.text: Chaining, because it calls the model several times in a row
choices.why: The number and order of calls in a chain are fixed in code.

choices.text: Orchestrator and workers
choices.why: Right. The amount of work is decided at run time, which is half of what an agent does.

choices.text: Routing, because the model's label changes what runs next
choices.why: The model chooses once, among branches the programmer wrote, and never sees a result.

choices.text: Parallelisation, since it runs calls at once
choices.why: Running at once is about speed. The calls and their number are fixed.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend reaching for a workflow pattern before an agent?

choices.text: Because agents are not yet supported by the major providers' APIs
choices.why: Every major provider supports tool calls, which is all an agent needs.

choices.text: Because a workflow always gives better answers
choices.why: Section 05 shows the router giving a worse answer to Bia than the agent did.

choices.text: Its failures have an address and its cost a sum known beforehand
choices.why: Right. You wrote every path, so a failure points at a step and the cost adds up in advance.

choices.text: Because workflows need no model calls
choices.why: All five patterns are arrangements of model calls.

prompt: How many requests did the agent send to the model for lesson 1's three messages, as `tally.py` counted them?
The router answered Bia with `M-1042 is delivered, delivered on 2026-09-24`. What went wrong?

choices.text: The model misread the message and returned the wrong label
choices.why: `order` is a fair label for a message about an order. The problem is what the branch does with it.

choices.text: No branch covers a return question about one order
choices.why: Right. The order branch prints the status; nothing in the code works out a return window.

choices.text: get_order returned an out-of-date delivery date
choices.why: The date matches shop.db and the agent's answer.

choices.text: The router ran out of tokens
choices.why: Five output tokens are plenty for a one-word label, and the label arrived.

prompt: The tallies show 2.0 s of model time for the router and 37.4 s for the agent, on a small model with no graphics chip. Which conclusion carries over to a paid provider?

choices.text: That the agent will be about eighteen times slower than the router
choices.why: The ratio depends on this machine and this model. A provider's timing differs, and so would yours.

choices.text: None, because a local model's timings say nothing about any other
choices.why: The seconds do not carry over, but the requests and tokens behind them would be sent to any model.

choices.text: More, larger requests, and more tokens written
choices.why: Right. The shape, more and larger requests and longer outputs, holds with any provider; the exact ratio does not.

choices.text: That routers are always faster
choices.why: A router with a slow branch, or a large model, is not. The comparison is this router against this agent.

prompt: The courier complaint went to `[other] passed to a person`. Why does the lesson treat that branch as valuable?

choices.text: It counts what no branch covers
choices.why: Right. The number of times 'other' fires measures how much a fixed path misses.

choices.text: It is the cheapest branch, since no lookup runs
choices.why: Cheap, but that is not why it matters.

choices.text: Complaints must never be answered by software
choices.why: The lesson draws no such rule. The point is what the branch measures.

choices.text: It hides the router's mistakes
choices.why: It does the opposite: it makes the misses visible and countable.

prompt: Each step of a run is right with probability 0.95, independently. To two decimal places, what is the chance that all 10 steps are right?
A tool that refuses bad arguments turns a wrong step into an error the model sees. Why does that help the whole run so much?

choices.text: Because an error message costs fewer tokens to send than a full result does
choices.why: An error message and a result cost about the same tokens.

choices.text: Each step's accuracy rises, and the run multiplies them
choices.why: Right. A caught mistake is corrected instead of built on, and every factor in the product rises.

choices.text: Because the model stops the run whenever any tool reports an error
choices.why: Stopping is one option; correcting and continuing is the one that helps the product.

choices.text: It makes the steps independent
choices.why: Independence is the table's simplifying assumption, not something a check creates.

prompt: Lesson 1 asked the agent about M-1043 and it looked the order up; this lesson asked the same and it searched the help centre. What does the table in this section say that means for a run of ten steps?

choices.text: Nothing, because a question asked twice is only one step each time
choices.why: It is one step here, and the same uncertainty sits in every step of a longer run.

choices.text: Each step's chance of going right is below 1, and ten of them multiply
choices.why: Right. A step that varies between runs has an accuracy below 1, and a chain of them compounds it.

choices.text: The search was a better choice, so longer runs will improve
choices.why: Searching for an order id in the help centre was the worse choice: the order holds the answer.

choices.text: Ollama changed the model between the two lessons
choices.why: Both runs used llama3.2:3b with the same tag. The model chose differently.

prompt: Which of Marginalia's tools is in the 'reads' row, the one an agent can be given most freely?

choices.text: refund, as long as the amount is small
choices.why: A small refund is still money that has to be taken back by another transaction.

choices.text: search_help
choices.why: Right. Searching again is free, and nothing reaches the world.

choices.text: A tool that emails the customer a confirmation
choices.why: An email is external and cannot be unsent.

choices.text: A tool that cancels an order that has not shipped
choices.why: Cancelling has a cost to reverse, even before shipping: the customer has to order again.

prompt: Why does the lesson call an agent that stops and asks the cheaper failure for writes that cost money?

choices.text: A wrong refusal costs a message; a wrong refund costs money
choices.why: Right. The two errors are not symmetric, and the design should lean towards the cheaper one.

choices.text: Because people are faster than agents at deciding whether a refund is due
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; the cost of each kind of mistake is.

choices.text: Because asking is required by consumer law in every country
choices.why: The argument is about cost, and it holds without any law behind it.

choices.text: Because models never get refunds right
choices.why: Models get many right. The point is what each wrong one costs.

prompt: What does 'moving a tool up the table' mean in practice?

choices.text: Listing it first for the model
choices.why: The order of tool definitions does not change what an action costs to undo.

choices.text: Requiring two approvals instead of one before the tool runs
choices.why: That guards the tool where it is. Moving it changes what the action is.

choices.text: Rebuilding the action so that undoing it is possible: a hold, a draft, a soft delete
choices.why: Right. A hold instead of a cancellation, a draft instead of a send: the same goal, a cheaper mistake.

choices.text: Running the tool on a faster server
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with reversibility.

prompt: Why did 'let the agent issue refunds for damaged books' become a workflow with the refund behind a person's confirmation?

choices.text: Because the help centre has no article about damaged books, so the policy is unclear
choices.why: It has one, h12, and it is clear: photographs within 14 days, replacement at no cost.

choices.text: Because an agent cannot read photographs at all
choices.why: Whether a model can read a photo is beside the point; the design question is who decides the payment.

choices.text: Because refunds are handled by the bank and not by the shop
choices.why: shop.py records refunds itself; the shop decides them.

choices.text: The check is a rule, and the payment is costly to reverse
choices.why: Right. Most of the path is a rule, and the one costly action gets a person in front of it.

prompt: Which of the five proposals became an agent, and with which tools?

choices.text: Order status, with get_order and a refund tool
choices.why: Order status is one lookup and a template: a workflow.

choices.text: The router's leftovers, read-only
choices.why: Right. The cases no branch covers, read-only, with a person reviewing before anything is sent.

choices.text: The stock report, because it runs every night
choices.why: Running every night says nothing about the path, which is fixed.

choices.text: Password questions
choices.why: One article answers them every time.

prompt: Put the steps of deciding whether to build an agent in the order this lesson works through them.
items: Ask whether the path can be written down
Ask what a wrong step costs and whether it can be undone
Ask whether the result can be checked
Ask whether the volume and deadline allow it

prompt: In Anthropic's vocabulary, a system whose paths are written in code is a ___, even when every step calls a model.
